content: The section provides a detailed analysis of qualitative evidence synthesis findings that are general in nature and not tied to any specific intervention or class of intervention. These findings were utilized by the Guideline Development Group (GDG), alongside their own expertise, to make judgments across various Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) domains. Findings 1–5 are general and applicable to all interventions, while findings 6–10 pertain to medicines, 11–17 to physical interventions, 18–20 to psychological interventions, and finding 21 to educational interventions. The synthesis included 22 studies (24 reports) involving 580 older adults, with 14 studies exclusively involving participants aged 60 years or older. Five studies had a mean or median participant age of 60 years or older, and three studies specifically sampled populations from lowand middle-income countries or vulnerable populations. No studies explored the perceptions or experiences of caregivers, whether formal or informal. The studies were conducted in seven high-income countries (United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Sweden, Australia, Canada, and Chile), one upper middle-income country (Brazil), and one lower middle-income country (Nigeria). No studies were identified from low-income countries. Most data were derived from cohorts with a mean age of 60 years or older. Older adults expressed clear preferences for treatments that were effective, credible, tailored to their individual needs, and aimed at improving their function. They valued individualized, person-centered care and expected treatments to be safe, accessible, and cost-effective. Treatments that reduced or relieved pain temporarily and improved long-term function were particularly valued. Older adults emphasized the importance of individualized care and guidance, whether delivered by health practitioners or peers. They appreciated person-centered care and felt safer when supervision or professional guidance was provided. However, the burden of accessing care, including treatment costs, travel time, and distance, was a significant barrier for many. High costs often rendered treatments inaccessible or deterred older adults from continuing recommended treatments. Proximity to healthcare providers was also a critical factor, as chronic pain limited their ability to travel long distances. Services located far away were perceived as insufficient or inaccessible, although some participants were willing to travel for trusted or preferred healthcare providers or to explore new treatment options. In terms of equity, older adults in countries with subsidized treatment costs or insurance discussed cost barriers less frequently than those who had to pay out-of-pocket for services. None of the studies reported on the general acceptability or feasibility of interventions. The GDG formulated recommendations for interventions based on available evidence, considering factors such as user values, resource requirements, equity, human rights, acceptability, and feasibility. Where evidence was insufficient, key considerations were provided to guide clinical practice. Structured and standardized educational interventions were defined as those aiming to improve understanding of chronic primary low back pain (CPLBP) and guide self-management and well-being. These interventions were distinct from personalized advice provided during clinical encounters. Educational interventions could be delivered through various media (verbal, written, digital) and formats (individual or group), with local contextual factors influencing the mode of delivery. The GDG conditionally recommended offering structured and standardized education and advice as part of care for adults, including older adults, with CPLBP, despite very low certainty evidence. These interventions typically included at least two topics, such as exercise and helping individuals make sense of their CPLBP experience.
